section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Differential equations are laws written as derivatives. In this chapter, we learned to read those laws in several ways:
Each method is useful. Each method also has a danger.
Before leaving differential equations, we collect three warnings. They are not side remarks. They protect the meaning of the whole chapter.
section.md: \text{A differential equation is not complete without enough starting information.}

note.md: \text{For which constant values of \(y\) does this expression equal zero?}
note.p: Those values are candidates for equilibrium solutions.

subsection.p: This is not only a technical warning. In models, equilibrium solutions often carry the main interpretation. Extinction, carrying capacity, room temperature, and chemical balance all appear as constant solutions.
Losing them would lose the story.

exercise.title: Why can algebra lose the most important solutions?

statement.p: Separation often begins by dividing by an expression involving y. In your own words, why are the values that make that expression zero often the equilibria of a model, and what story is lost if they are discarded?

hint.p: Extinction, carrying capacity, and room temperature appear as constant solutions. Check those candidates before dividing them away.

warning.title: Numerical warning
warning.p: A numerical method has its own behavior. It is not the same object as the differential equation.
Before trusting a numerical solution, check whether it agrees with the qualitative behavior of the equation.

subsection.p: So solutions are pushed toward 0. A numerical solution that shoots away from 0 is suspect.
This is why numerical methods and direction fields belong together. The direction field does not give exact values, but it can catch a numerical approximation that is following the wrong story.

exercise.title: Why can Euler’s method follow the wrong story?

statement.p: A differential equation may describe stable decay while a large Euler step produces growing oscillations. In your own words, why is the numerical method not the same object as the equation, and how can a direction field catch the false behavior?

hint.p: The method has its own dynamics. Before trusting a table of values, ask whether they agree with the qualitative arrows of the field.

subsection.title: Same differential equation, different initial conditions
subsection.p: A differential equation gives a law of change. It does not usually give a single history.
Different constants C give different solution curves.
This solution starts below 1 and rises toward 1.
This solution starts above 1 and falls toward 1.
The same equation gives all three behaviors. The initial condition selects which one happens.

figure.caption: The equation y'=1-y gives a family. The initial condition selects one solution.

subsection.p: For a first-order equation, one initial condition usually chooses one solution curve. For a second-order equation, one initial condition is usually not enough.
But C_2 is still free. Both functions
They differ because their initial velocities differ:
A second-order motion needs position and velocity.

note.title: Initial data rule
note.p: A differential equation gives the rule of motion. Initial conditions give the starting state.
A first-order equation usually needs one starting value. A second-order equation usually needs two: position and velocity.

subsection.p: This is why a spring cannot be described by its position alone. If the mass is at equilibrium, it may stay there, or it may be passing through with high speed. The position is the same. The future is not.

exercise.title: Why is a differential equation incomplete without enough starting information?

statement.p: The same first-order equation can describe many histories, and a second-order spring needs both position and velocity. In your own words, what does the differential equation determine, what do initial conditions determine, and why can two masses at the same place have different futures?

hint.p: The equation is the rule of motion. Initial data choose the starting state. A first-order law usually needs one starting value; a second-order law usually needs two.

subsection.title: The three warnings together
subsection.p: The warnings can be remembered as three questions.

row.cell: Did we divide by an expression that might be zero?
We may have lost equilibrium solutions.
Is a numerical step size too large?
Euler’s method may create false oscillation or false growth.
Have we supplied enough initial information?
The differential equation may describe a family, not one solution.

subsection.p: Differential equations are powerful because they describe change locally. That same local nature makes them sensitive to algebraic assumptions, numerical choices, and initial data.
The chapter ends by gathering the main methods and putting them back to work in applications.
